title: FRM Operational, Lesson 4: Scenario analysis - measuring what has never happened
subtitle: Internal data can only tell you about what has already occurred, and the tail by definition has not
whyItMatters: The loss distribution approach needs data, yet the most severe operational events are so rare that no institution has a sufficient sample. Scenario analysis is the only tool that reaches that region, and it is also the part of the operational risk framework most easily reduced to a formality.
openingQuestion: A bank has 12 years of internal loss data, the largest event being 40bn. It wants to estimate the loss at the 99.9% level. Which approach is sound?
openingOptions: Extrapolate the distribution fitted to 12 years of data straight out to the 99.9% level
Combine internal data, industry data and scenarios
Take the largest event in the 12 years and multiply it by a safety factor of 3
Ignore the tail, since there is no statistical basis on which to estimate it
explanation: The 99.9% level corresponds to a once-in-a-thousand-year event. Twelve years of data contains no observation in that region, so any number extrapolated out there is a product of the distribution family chosen rather than of the data. Basel therefore requires four sources: internal loss data, external data, scenario analysis, and business environment and internal control factors. Scenarios are the only source that can speak about things that have never happened to that particular institution.

diagram.label: Internal data - thick in the body, empty in the tail
External data - it has a tail, but somebody else's
Scenario analysis - builds a tail for your own institution
Combine into one distribution usable for capital and for planning

realWorldExample.company: A bank building a large-scale internal fraud scenario
realWorldExample.description: A good scenario workshop does not open with the question of how large the loss would be. It opens with the sequence of events: who could do this, which control checkpoints would they pass, how long before detection, and how large would the position be over that window. The money figure is only the final output; the real value lies in the group realising which control checkpoint genuinely stops nothing.

quiz.question: Why is internal loss data not sufficient for estimating the tail?
options: Because older losses no longer reflect the firm's current size
Because internal data is always recorded somewhat inaccurately
Because Basel does not allow internal data to be used for the tail
Because tail events are so rare they never appear in the sample
quiz.explanation: Ten years of data holds many small events and a few medium ones, and almost never a catastrophic one. Fitting a distribution and then extrapolating to the 99.9% level means the final number is decided by the distribution family - switching from lognormal to Pareto can multiply the result several times over without a single row of data changing. Internal data is in fact the source Basel weights most heavily, and staleness and recording error are real issues that better housekeeping fixes; the emptiness of the tail is not fixable that way.

quiz.question: What separates a valuable scenario workshop from a formality?
options: It forces a description of the event chain and which control failed
It has the participation of the most senior leaders in the firm
It produces a loss number precise to the nearest billion dong
It is run the minimum number of times the rules require each year
quiz.explanation: The money figure is the easiest output and the least valuable one. What is worth having is the walk through each step: who could do this, which checkpoint should have stopped it, why it did not. Many institutions find a control gap during the meeting itself, before any number exists. Senior attendance and an annual count are inputs that a purely ceremonial session satisfies just as easily, and false precision in the loss estimate is a warning sign rather than a mark of quality.

quiz.question: What are the four data sources Basel requires for an operational risk framework?
options: Internal loss data, internal audit, external audit, and management reporting
Internal loss, external loss, scenarios, and business environment factors
Market data, credit data, operational data, and human resources data
Scenarios, stress testing, backtesting, and model sensitivity analysis
quiz.explanation: The four sources cover each other's weaknesses: internal data is close to the institution but empty in the tail, external data has a tail but somebody else's, scenarios build a tail for your own firm but are subjective, and environment and control factors keep the number reflecting the present rather than the past. The other lists name real activities that are either assurance functions or model validation techniques - useful work, but none of them generates loss severity data.

quiz.question: Which bias threatens the results of scenario analysis most?
options: Participants lack sufficient technical expertise in the models
The group always estimates losses above the realistic level
Anchoring on the most recent incident the group remembers
The input data is rounded off before it enters the calculation
quiz.explanation: After an incident, every scenario circles that same kind of incident and the loss estimates cling to the figure that just materialised. In the other direction, several quiet years and the scenarios shrink. That is why an independent facilitator is needed, and a cross-check against industry data - to work against the group's own memory. Note that the bias runs in both directions rather than always upward, and that it is a property of recall rather than of modelling skill or rounding.

quiz.question: Scenario: A group estimates a scenario with a frequency of once in 20 years and a loss of 500bn. What is the expected annual loss?
options: 20bn/year (= using the year count as the loss)
500bn/year (= taking the scenario's loss amount as it stands)
10,000bn/year (= 500 × 20, multiplying instead of dividing)
25bn/year (= 500 ÷ 20, frequency times severity)
quiz.explanation: The expected annual loss is frequency times severity: (1/20) × 500 = 25bn. That number is used to compare scenarios against one another, but do not read it as a forecast - in 19 years the loss is 0 and in one year it is 500bn, and no year is ever 25.

practicePrompt.question: After a major cyber incident elsewhere in the industry, the bank's scenario workshop raises its cyber loss estimate from 200bn to 900bn while leaving every other scenario unchanged. What is worrying here?
options: Anchoring on the most recent incident, so the other scenarios are forgotten
The 900bn figure is too large relative to the bank's capital base
Scenarios should not be revised mid-cycle, but at next year's review
Raising the estimate is right, but all four data sources should rise together
practicePrompt.explanation: Anchoring on the most recent incident is the most dangerous bias in scenario analysis, and its signature is exactly the shape seen here: one scenario swelling fourfold while every other one stands still. What genuinely changes after an industry incident is not the probability of that one event type, but the understanding of the event chain and of which control checkpoints can fail together - and that lesson usually applies to several other scenarios too. This is also why the value of a workshop lies in the event chain and the control checkpoints rather than in the money figure: the number gets anchored, the mechanism does not.

keyTakeaways: Internal data is thick in the body and empty in the tail; extrapolating to 99.9% lets the distribution family decide the result
Basel requires four sources: internal loss, external loss, scenarios, and business environment and control factors
The value of a scenario workshop lies in the event chain and the failed control checkpoints, not in the money figure
The most dangerous bias is anchoring on the most recent incident - scenarios swell after one and shrink after quiet years

summary.keyIdea: Scenario analysis is the only way to speak about the tail when the tail has never happened to you. It is subjective, and precisely because it is subjective the process matters more than the number.

application.message: When you read a scenario report, find the event chain narrative rather than stopping at the table of numbers. A scenario that cannot say which control checkpoint failed has not finished its job.

sections.text: Operational risk capital is usually computed at the 99.9% confidence level - a once-in-a-thousand-year event. The uncomfortable question: where does data about something nobody has ever seen come from?

A fifteen-year-old institution has fifteen years of data, most of it small events. Fitting a distribution to that and stretching it out to 99.9% is technically valid and almost meaningless in information terms: the final number is decided by the distribution family chosen, not by the data. Swap lognormal for Pareto and the result can multiply several times over without a single row of data changing.
Four sources, each patching one hole

Internal data is right for you but empty in the tail. Industry data has a tail, but it is another institution's tail, at another scale, with other controls. Scenarios build a tail for your own firm but depend on human judgement. Business environment and control factors keep the picture reflecting the present rather than the institution of five years ago.
Why the process matters more than the number

A good scenario workshop forces the group through each step: who could do this, which checkpoint would they pass, how long before detection, how much damage accumulates over that window. Very often the answer to the second question silences the room - and that is the real value, arriving before any number does.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: Scenarios swell immediately after an incident and shrink after a few quiet years. Both directions are memory bias rather than a change in real risk, so an independent facilitator and a reference point from industry data are both needed.
